newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Data give Australian dlr bulls bad case of deja vu.
newsitem.headline: Data give Australian dlr bulls bad case of deja vu.

text.p: The Australian dollar shuddered backwards Thursday as dismal retail sales figures stirred unhappy memories for many a bull.

Sales slid 1.8 percent in June, the biggest drop in nine months, to confound market forecasts of a 0.4 percent rise. It meant sales for the June quarter were down 0.5 percent in real terms implying a detraction from GDP growth.

Dealers remembered it was a shock 1.7 percent fall in April sales which first sparked talk about a fifth rate cut, which was finally delivered just Wednesday, and left them wondering if the whole speculative circus could start once again.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the dollar had drifted to US$0.7433/38 from US$0.7460/65 late here Wednesday.
The latter had been the best finish in three weeks and raised bullish hopes the currency could wear the reality of lower official interest rates after weeks of anticipation.

Part of the equanimity was due to the widespread assumption official rates had now bottomed at 5.0 percent as there was enough monetary stimulus in the pipeline to assure a pickup in growth to the four percent level needed to curb unemployment.
That was still the feeling of most analysts, although the dire sales data did not make it easy to be confident about it.

"Today's report presents a surprisingly weak picture of consumer spending, which is at odds with some of the anecdotal evidence from major retailers," said Andrew Pease, a senior economist at Nomura Research.

He noted the figures were notoriously volatile and suspected monthly seasonal factors might not be adequately accounting for changing patterns in store sales -- many department stors delayed sales to July from June.
Lower interest rates should also help promote spending in the second half of the year, he said, noting the rate cut from May 23 was only passed on to existing borrowers this week.
Others felt the figures were just a taste of the disappointment to come.
"The numbers are consistent with our view that economic and employment growth will remain subdued over coming months," said John Peters, a senior economist at Westpac.
"This moderate growth scenario, against the backdrop of a very benign inflation outlook, leaves the door open for another cut in official cash rates in late 1997," he said.
In paticular, analysts reckoned it would take a string of stronger employment numbers before consumers felt secure enough about their jobs to spend more.
That made next week's labour report all the more crucial.
Analysts said employment was overdue a big bounce after surprising weakness in recent months but the volatility of the series is such that noone was confident of strength.
Treasurer Peter Costello was upbeat on the prospects for stronger economic growth in 1997/98 in a conference speech today and predicted this would bring down unemployment over time.

He also expected underlying inflation to remain around 2.0 percent, the floor of the RBA's target range, for the entire financial year. To the market, this implied there would be room for another easing should the economy disappoint.
Dealers said the lingering uncertainty over rates would make it hard for the dollar to sustain a recovery above major resistance in the US$0.7530/7550 range.
Nevertheless, support had been solid at US$0.7420 so far and most felt last week's 18-month low of US$0.7310 had probably marked the end of its four month-old downtrend.

On the crosses the dollar dipped to 87.60/70 yen from Wednesday's late 88.74/84. It also lost some of its recent gains on the mark to 1.3642/65 from 1.3723/45 -- which had been the highest close in more than five years -- but was unchanged in trade weighted terms at 58.3. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
